planting.note: Also sowable in autumn in mild climates for an overwintered crop; direct sow as soon as soil can be worked.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep into cool, workable soil as early as late winter, spacing plants close together so they support each other without staking. This RHS Award of Garden Merit variety is prized by British allotment growers for pods near a foot long holding six or seven large, flavorful beans that freeze especially well, and pinching the growing tips once the lowest flower trusses set pods helps deter aphids and encourages even filling.

planting.note: Can also be sown in October-November in mild winter regions for an early spring crop.

directions: Sow directly into fertile, moisture-retentive soil and support the tall, square-stemmed plants with stakes and string along the row in exposed gardens. Another RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, this heavy-cropping English heirloom produces pods to about a foot long packed with up to nine green-skinned beans, and its scented black-and-white flowers make it one of the more ornamental vegetables in a spring kitchen garden.

Give this vigorous English show-bench heirloom sturdy staking since its thick, fleshy pods can reach 12 inches and weigh the plant down as they fill with up to 10 light greenish-white beans each. It remains a favorite on the British show bench for sheer pod length, but home cooks value it just as much for the buttery, nutty flavor of beans harvested young and steamed whole in the pod.

Sow this compact, container-friendly broad bean close together in rich soil and start picking pods early while they are still flat and only a few inches long. Bred specifically for a thin, tender pod wall rather than for the beans inside, Stereo can be snapped and eaten whole like a mangetout pea, though left longer it also yields a conventional crop of sweet, nutty-flavored shelled beans.

Plant this short, sturdy, wind-tolerant broad bean in a sunny bed, raised bed, or even a large container, since compact plants rarely need staking. Marketed by Suttons as the first broad bean created especially for eating in the pod, Statissa carries thin, short pods with small, delicate beans that can be steamed whole like mangetout, and it earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit for reliable, heavy early-summer cropping.

planting.note: Bred for autumn sowing in mild-winter regions; can also be spring sown in colder zones.

directions: In mild-winter regions sow in fall for a fresh-eating spring crop; this fava shrugs off cold that collapses other varieties, making it a reliable overwintering cover and food crop in one. It is named for fava collector and natural-building pioneer Ianto Evans, and its pods carry seeds ranging from pale green to dark purple and mauve, all good at the green-shell or dry-bean stage, with the young shoot tips also edible as a salad green.

Sow thickly and thin to final spacing; this open-pollinated Swiss kohlrabi, listed by the heirloom seed house Sativa Rheinau and the ProSpecieRara conservation network, forms smooth, pale-green globes with notably thin, tender skin that rarely needs peeling even at full size. Because it's open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, seed can be saved from year to year, and succession sowing every two to three weeks keeps a steady supply of crisp, juicy bulbs for slaws through a long cool season.

Keep soil evenly moist as the pale-green, flattened-round bulbs size up to about six inches across, since inconsistent watering is the usual cause of woody or split kohlrabi. This Sakata hybrid's dark, upright leaves and slow-to-bolt habit make it forgiving of a slightly delayed harvest, and the white interior flesh stays sweet and crisp whether eaten raw in slaws or roasted like a root vegetable.

Thin seedlings early so bulbs have room to swell into their characteristic semi-globe shape, which at nearly a pound still holds tender, non-fibrous flesh if harvested promptly. This pale-green hybrid is a dependable market-garden standard for bulk production because the whole planting matures within a tight window, simplifying one-pass harvest.

An open-pollinated Swiss heirloom from the Roggli family of Hilterfingen rather than a modern hybrid, Lanro is worth growing for seed-saving gardeners who want a true-breeding kohlrabi alongside its F1 competitors. Compact plants form tender green bulbs weighing roughly half a pound, best picked while still young since open-pollinated kohlrabi tends to toughen faster than hybrids once past peak size.

Direct sow once soil has warmed in late spring, since this short, bushy soybean was bred in Fiskeby, Norrkoping, Sweden, by Dr. Sven Holmberg specifically to set and finish pods reliably in cool, short-growing-season climates where most edamame struggle. Harvest at the green-shell stage when pods are plump but still bright green for sweet, crunchy edamame, or leave them to dry fully for a high-protein dry soybean.

Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, giving this vigorous bush soybean full sun and consistent moisture through pod fill. Developed as a food-grade variety for the edamame trade, BeSweet 292 was one of the cultivars studied in University of Illinois machine-harvest density trials and reliably fills pods with two to three large, flavorful beans prized for steaming and salting straight from the pod.

planting.note: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a frost-sweetened fall and winter storage crop.

directions: Direct sow in mid to late summer so roots size up through the cooling days of fall, when frost converts starches to sugars and mellows typical rutabaga bite. Bred in Maine by Radcliffe Pike from an interspecific cross with Chinese cabbage, this variety has purple-topped white skin reminiscent of Laurentian but a notably fine-grained, sweeter yellow flesh, and it stores exceptionally well in a cold root cellar.
